title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP
short: All provide core compute, networking, storage and managed services; requirements drive selection.
answer: Compare ecosystem fit, skills, regions, security, cost and managed services.
interview: All provide core compute, networking, storage and managed services; requirements drive selection.

title: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
short: Vertical adds resources to an instance; horizontal adds instances.
answer: Horizontal scaling requires appropriate state management and traffic distribution.
interview: Vertical adds resources to an instance; horizontal adds instances.

title: Load balancer
short: It distributes traffic across healthy instances.
answer: It may perform health checks, L4/L7 routing and TLS termination depending on product.
interview: It distributes traffic across healthy instances.

title: Container
short: A container packages an application and dependencies while sharing the host kernel.
answer: Containers improve deployment consistency but are not identical to VMs in isolation characteristics.
interview: A container packages an application and dependencies while sharing the host kernel.

title: Kubernetes high level
short: Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads using desired state.
answer: Pods run workloads, Services provide stable networking and Deployments manage replicas/rollouts.
interview: Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads using desired state.

title: Readiness vs liveness
short: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness controls restart decisions.
answer: A process can be alive but temporarily not ready. Avoid fragile deep liveness checks.
interview: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness controls restart decisions.

title: Autoscaling
short: Autoscaling changes capacity based on workload signals.
answer: It can use CPU, memory, request rate or custom metrics; downstream bottlenecks remain possible.
interview: Autoscaling changes capacity based on workload signals.

title: Object storage
short: It stores blobs as objects addressed by keys.
answer: Use for documents/images/backups; store transactional searchable metadata in a database.
interview: It stores blobs as objects addressed by keys.

title: Infrastructure as code
short: Infrastructure is declared in version-controlled files.
answer: IaC improves reproducibility and reviewability while reducing drift.
interview: Infrastructure is declared in version-controlled files.

title: Secure cloud backend
short: Use least-privilege identity, encryption, secret management, private networking and audit logs.
answer: Prefer workload identities/roles over static keys and use layered network/application controls.
interview: Use least-privilege identity, encryption, secret management, private networking and audit logs.

title: What is a container image?
short: An image is an immutable packaged filesystem and metadata used to create containers.
answer: A Dockerfile describes image build steps. Containers are runtime instances of images, with writable runtime layers and isolated processes. Images should be small, reproducible and free of unnecessary secrets.
followups: How do you reduce image size?
mistakes: Baking secrets into images.
Treating a container as a lightweight virtual machine with its own full kernel.
interview: A container image packages the application and its dependencies; a container is a running instance using the host kernel and container isolation.

title: What is a Kubernetes Deployment?
short: A Deployment manages a desired number of pod replicas and supports controlled rollouts and rollbacks.
answer: The Deployment describes a pod template and replica count. Kubernetes creates ReplicaSets and replaces pods to converge on the desired state.
code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: backend:1.2
mistakes: Exposing a Deployment directly as a stable network endpoint.
Assuming a pod IP is permanent.
interview: A Deployment manages application replicas and rollout state. A Service provides stable networking to the selected pods.

title: What is a Kubernetes Service?
short: A Service provides a stable virtual endpoint and load balances traffic to matching pods.
answer: Pods are ephemeral, so clients should not depend on pod IPs. A Service selects pods using labels and provides stable DNS and networking semantics.
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  selector:
    app: orders
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
followups: How does service discovery work in Kubernetes?
mistakes: Treating Service as a process running inside the pod.
Selecting pods with incorrect labels.
interview: A Kubernetes Service gives stable discovery and routing to changing pod instances.

title: What is autoscaling?
short: Autoscaling changes compute capacity based on demand or resource signals.
answer: Horizontal scaling adds instances or pods; vertical scaling increases resources per instance. Good autoscaling needs meaningful metrics, cooldown behavior and protection against oscillation.
code:
HPA: desiredReplicas = metric / target
// Kubernetes adjusts pod count
followups: Why can CPU be a poor autoscaling metric?
mistakes: Assuming more instances always fix latency.
Scaling on a metric unrelated to actual bottleneck.
interview: Autoscaling adjusts capacity as demand changes. I choose the scaling dimension and signal based on the workload and verify that downstream dependencies can scale too.

title: What is a VPC or virtual network?
short: It is an isolated logical network in a cloud environment containing subnets, routes and security controls.
answer: A typical design separates public and private subnets, places load balancers at appropriate boundaries and keeps databases private. Exact components vary by provider.
code: Internet -> public load balancer -> private application subnet -> private database subnet
mistakes: Putting databases directly on public subnets without need.
Treating network isolation as sufficient application authorization.
interview: A cloud virtual network defines routing and network boundaries. I combine private placement with identity and application-layer authorization.

title: What is IAM?
short: Identity and Access Management controls who or what can access cloud resources and what actions are allowed.
answer: IAM typically uses identities, roles, policies and temporary credentials. Least privilege means granting only required actions on required resources.
code:
Role -> policy -> allow
resource: storage://orders/*
action: read
mistakes: Using root or administrator credentials for applications.
Granting wildcard permissions everywhere.
interview: IAM provides identity and authorization for cloud resources. I prefer workload roles and short-lived credentials with least privilege.

title: What is a managed database?
short: A managed database delegates operational tasks such as provisioning, patching, backups and failover to the cloud provider.
answer: Managed does not mean no responsibility. The application still owns schema, indexes, query behavior, credentials, data lifecycle and recovery objectives.
code:
Application -> managed PostgreSQL
                 provider handles patching/backups
mistakes: Assuming the provider guarantees application-level correctness.
Skipping backup restore testing.
interview: Managed databases reduce operational work but do not remove engineering responsibility for performance, security, backups and recovery testing.

title: What is blue-green deployment?
short: Blue-green deployment maintains two environments and switches traffic from the old version to the new version after validation.
answer: The inactive environment receives the new release. After smoke tests, routing changes to it. Rollback can be fast by switching traffic back, provided database changes are backward compatible.
code:
Blue: v1 <- traffic
Green: v2 <- deploy/test
Switch traffic -> Green
followups: How do you handle database schema changes?
mistakes: Ignoring database compatibility during rollback.
Calling a canary deployment blue-green.
interview: Blue-green reduces release switching risk by keeping old and new environments available. Database changes must support both versions during the transition.

title: How would you design Kubernetes autoscaling for a Java API?
short: Scale on demand/saturation signals while respecting startup time and downstream capacity.
answer: CPU may miss I/O saturation. Combine appropriate metrics, set min/max replicas, use readiness and graceful termination, and cap scale-out to protect the database.
followups: How do you prevent scale oscillation?
mistakes: Scaling only on CPU for an I/O-bound service.
interview: Autoscaling is a capacity loop. I choose signals tied to demand and verify that dependencies can absorb the additional load.

title: How do you design Kubernetes liveness/readiness correctly?
short: Readiness controls traffic; liveness detects unrecoverable process failure; startup probes protect slow initialization.
answer: A dependency outage should generally affect readiness rather than trigger liveness restarts. Probes should be cheap and representative of their purpose.
mistakes: Putting fragile downstream checks in liveness.
interview: I keep probe semantics separate so a transient database outage does not restart every pod and create a second incident.

title: How do you debug Kubernetes OOMKills for Java?
short: Compare container RSS with heap, metaspace, direct buffers, thread stacks and native memory.
answer: The container can be killed even when Java heap is below Xmx. Leave headroom for non-heap memory and inspect cgroup limits and GC behavior.
mistakes: Setting Xmx equal to the pod limit.
interview: I distinguish Java heap OOM from container OOMKill. The JVM and native libraries need memory outside the heap.

title: How do you design safe Kubernetes rolling releases?
short: Combine compatible application/database versions, readiness, graceful shutdown and controlled rollout parameters.
answer: Mixed versions must work together. Use readiness gates, termination grace periods, maxSurge/maxUnavailable and automated rollback signals.
mistakes: Incompatible schema changes during rolling deployment.
interview: A Kubernetes rollout is only safe if the application and schema are backward compatible during coexistence.

title: How do you design disaster recovery for a backend?
short: Define RPO/RTO first, then choose backups/replication and recovery procedures that meet them.
answer: Stateless services can be rebuilt from immutable artifacts; data requires tested backups or replication. Include DNS, secrets, dependencies and external providers in the recovery plan.
code:
RPO=5m; RTO=30m
// validate through restore drills
mistakes: Designing DR without RPO/RTO targets.
interview: I start with business recovery objectives and test restores/failover rather than assuming backups are usable.

title: How do you control noisy-neighbor behavior in cloud systems?
short: Enforce per-tenant quotas, concurrency limits and resource isolation.
answer: Measure resource consumption by tenant and apply rate/queue/database budgets. Premium tenants may require dedicated partitions or compute.
followups: How do you handle premium tenants?
mistakes: Using only a global rate limit.
interview: Noisy-neighbor protection is capacity fairness. I enforce limits at the earliest useful boundary and observe usage by tenant.

title: How do you optimize cloud cost without harming reliability?
short: Optimize cost per useful unit of work while preserving SLOs and resilience.
answer: Rightsize compute, autoscale, manage storage/log retention and data transfer, and use committed capacity for predictable workloads. Track cost per request/tenant alongside latency and availability.
followups: How do you control log spend?
mistakes: Cutting redundancy or observability without measuring risk.
interview: I optimize measured cost per unit of business work, not by blindly choosing the cheapest infrastructure.

title: Kubernetes repeatedly OOMKills a Java service
short: Container memory is larger than Java heap; the process can be OOMKilled while heap is not full.
answer: I would compare container RSS with heap usage and account for metaspace, thread stacks, direct memory and native allocations. Then I would fix leaks or allocation pressure and size the JVM with explicit headroom inside the container limit.
code: Size JVM memory within the container limit, leaving headroom for non-heap/native memory. Investigate allocation or leaks before simply increasing the container limit. Set realistic requests/limits and test peak load.
followups: How does -Xmx relate to container limits?
How do you investigate native memory?
What is the difference between requests and limits?
mistakes: Setting Xmx equal to the container memory limit.
Assuming OOMKilled always means a Java heap leak.
interview: I would never infer container safety from heap usage alone. Kubernetes limits apply to the whole process.
scenario: A Java pod is stable under normal traffic but gets OOMKilled during peak load. The JVM heap appears below the configured heap maximum shortly before termination.
investigation: Compare container memory limit with JVM heap plus metaspace, thread stacks, native memory, direct buffers and other process overhead. Inspect container memory metrics and JVM native-memory data.
resolution: Size JVM memory within the container limit, leaving headroom for non-heap/native memory. Investigate allocation or leaks before simply increasing the container limit. Set realistic requests/limits and test peak load.
prevention: Monitor container RSS and JVM heap separately, alert before the limit and include container limits in JVM sizing decisions.

title: A rolling deployment causes capacity to drop below the SLO
short: Zero-downtime deployment depends on capacity, readiness and rollout policy together.
answer: I would ensure the rollout maintains enough ready capacity, usually with maxUnavailable set appropriately and maxSurge supported by cluster capacity. Readiness must prevent traffic from reaching unready pods.
code: Use readiness probes that reflect serving capability and configure rollout capacity so enough replicas remain available. For critical services, use maxUnavailable=0 where capacity permits and ensure cluster resources can support surge pods.
followups: How do readiness probes interact with deployments?
mistakes: Assuming rolling updates are automatically zero downtime.
Ignoring cluster capacity for surge pods.
interview: I would test deployments as production traffic events, not just application tests.
scenario: A service runs four pods. During rolling deployment, one old pod is terminated before a new pod becomes ready, leaving only three serving instances and causing latency spikes.
investigation: Inspect deployment strategy, maxUnavailable, maxSurge and readiness behavior. Compare available replicas with traffic and per-pod capacity.
resolution: Use readiness probes that reflect serving capability and configure rollout capacity so enough replicas remain available. For critical services, use maxUnavailable=0 where capacity permits and ensure cluster resources can support surge pods.
prevention: Load-test rollouts, monitor available replicas and latency during deployments and ensure the cluster has spare capacity for surge.

title: A Kubernetes HPA scales too late during traffic spikes
short: Autoscaling is constrained by detection time plus pod startup time; the metric must predict saturation early enough.
answer: I would measure the complete scaling loop. If CPU is delayed, I would consider request concurrency or queue depth, increase baseline capacity for known peaks and optimize pod startup time.
code: Use a metric that correlates earlier with saturation, such as request rate, concurrency or queue depth, and tune target utilization and startup capacity. Keep a minimum replica buffer for predictable peaks.
followups: When is queue depth a better metric?
How does cluster autoscaler interact with HPA?
mistakes: Choosing CPU because it is easy to measure.
Ignoring pod startup latency.
interview: I would tune autoscaling from the service’s actual bottleneck and response time, not blindly use CPU at 70 percent.
scenario: Traffic doubles in 30 seconds, but CPU-based HPA takes several minutes to add enough pods. p95 latency breaches the SLO before scaling completes.
investigation: Measure scale-up detection delay, pod startup time and whether CPU is a leading indicator for this workload. Check stabilization and metrics scrape intervals.
resolution: Use a metric that correlates earlier with saturation, such as request rate, concurrency or queue depth, and tune target utilization and startup capacity. Keep a minimum replica buffer for predictable peaks.
prevention: Load-test burst traffic, measure time-to-ready and set alerts on saturation before the SLO is breached.
